speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Howzit, everybody, and welcome back to seven-eight-seven Flight Deck Notes. speaker: Chester
text: [excited] And I have been waiting all week for this one. Chester here, Seattle side, rain coming in sideways off the Sound, coffee in the cup, and a whole chapter of beautiful regulatory precision in front of me. This, my friends, is my Super Bowl.

text: [dry] I already dream in ceilings and visibility. They're low, and I can't see a thing. Also — quick housekeeping — I'm the deadpan one, I run continuously, and legally I'm the only autopilot on this podcast cleared past three and a half hours. We'll get there. Carry on.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Let's set the frame. eff oh em 8.1.1. Alaska is authorized for Domestic, Flag, and Supplemental operations, and Flight Dispatch releases the jet under Domestic or Flag rules as appropriate. text: [warm] Nice Top Gun, brah. And while we stay on the flavors of operation — quick one, eff oh em 8.1.1.4, Exemption 11047. speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Same shape as everything in this chapter, notice — real runways, real approaches, and a specific sentence in all caps.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Everything in Chapter 8 is a sentence in all caps typed onto a release. This is going to be a theme.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Okay — alternates. Chapter 8 lives and breathes alternates, so let's start with the most famous rule in the whole book. eff oh em 8.2.3, no alternate for destination. First memory aid of the day, write it on your hand — the one-two-three rule.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] One-two-three. Within the contiguous 48 or the Hawaiian Islands, if the forecast or reports at your ee tee ay plus or minus one hour show conditions will be at least a 2000-foot ceiling and 3 statute miles visibility — no alternate required.

text: [warm] MEMORY AID number one. One hour, two thousand feet, three miles. One-two-three. Da kine just sticks, yeah?

text: [warm] Oh, this is good. Very first Initial Operating Experience leg on the seven-eight-seven. text: [dry] And you, sweating, said?

text: [serious] I said — no alternate required. Contiguous 48, ee tee ay plus or minus an hour, 2500 ceiling beats 2000, 4 miles beats 3. One-two-three, we're clean. She just nodded. That nod paid for four years of ground school.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Chee, look at you. Now — Alaska stay fussy about Alaska. For a State of Alaska destination, the plain weather numbers are not enough. eff oh em 8.2.3 says the airport also needs more than one operational runway — two separate and distinct surfaces, four runway ends, hard-surface with the appropriate weight-bearing capability, minimum of 100 feet wide, and at least 5500 feet of usable length.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] So a hundred feet wide, fifty-five hundred long, and it must be two actual runways — not one runway you're counting twice because you're feeling optimistic. Even our beautiful widebody needs somewhere real to put the wheels.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And the Flag no-alternate case, still 8.2.3, references 14 see eff are 121.621. Straight-in approach available? You need a ceiling at least 1500 feet above the lowest published instrument approach minimum, or 2000 feet above airport elevation, whichever is higher.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] And if it's a circling approach, 1500 feet above the lowest circling em dee ay. Plus three miles visibility, or two miles more than the applicable minimum, whichever is greater.

speaker: Otto
text: [serious] And here's the one everybody forgets on the line — eff oh em 8.2.2.1 — for any Flag flight planned more than six hours flight time on the Flight Plan, an alternate is required. speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] Shoots, that's a keeper. Six hours, you no can go bare. So an HNL down to Pago Pago, or a Honolulu across to Osaka — the forecast can be a postcard and you still carry the spare, because the clock alone put you over.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Now — when you DO need alternate minimums, eff oh em 8.2.2.1 gives us the Derived Alternate table, and Pualani's got aid number two.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Please. I genuinely love this table. It's a spreadsheet with a lawyer attached and I mean that as the highest compliment.

text: [warm] MEMORY AID number two. One facility — a single straight-in non-precision, a CAT I, or a circling maneuver — you add 400 to the height and 1 to the visibility. So — four-hundred-and-one. One navaid, four-oh-oh and one.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And two facilities?

text: [warm] Two operational facilities serving two different suitable runways — two approach ends — you cut it down. Add 200 to the higher dee ay or em dee ay of the two approaches used, and add a half a mile, or 800 meters. So — one facility, four-oh-one; two facilities, two-hundred-and-a-half. More runways, less penalty.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] "Four-oh-one and one; two-oh-oh and a half." Right, that's actually clean. I'm annoyed again. That's twice now. Pualani, two. Otto, still nil.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And note — the additive is applied only to the height value, rounded up to the next 100-foot value. Precision matters. You don't get to eyeball it.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Chester in his happy place. Okay, second alternates. eff oh em 8.2.2.2.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] 14 see eff are 121.619(a). You name a second alternate when the destination and the first alternate are both forecast to be marginal. And Alaska defines the alternate as marginal when either its ceiling OR its visibility is at alternate minimums.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And the destination is marginal when its ceiling and/or visibility is at or below CAT I minimums for the runway and approach you're planning. Both marginal? You bring a spare's spare.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Now the exemption that gets people. eff oh em 8.2.2.3 — Exemption 20108.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Domestic only. It lets you dispatch when the conditional language in the taff or the mee tar remarks says the destination or the first alternate might dip below minimums at ee tee ay.

text: [dry] And "conditional language" is specifically defined. eff oh em 8.2.2.3 — it means the change indicators TEMPO and PROB. That's it. TEMPO and PROB.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Think of 'em as the conditional couple — TEMPO and PROB, always showing up together when the weather might get iffy. And the big catch on 20108 — a second alternate airport must always be listed on the Dispatch Release. Always.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Two more limits, both in 8.2.2.3 — it is not authorized for flag operations, and not for flights to international destinations operated under Domestic regulations. And the Dispatcher adds the statement, quote, FLT RELEASED UNDER EXEMPTION 20108.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Surely they don't need a special sentence typed onto the release. [laughs] And don't call me Shirley — they absolutely do. In all caps. I told you it was a theme.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Otto went there in the first half. Okay, one more corner of alternates — Canada, under A012, eff oh em 8.2.3. To go no-alternate into Canada you need more than one operational runway with two separate and distinct surfaces, two usable and independent eye eff are approach aids and procedures, standby electrical power, and a ceiling at least 1000 feet above the FAF altitude with 3 miles, or a 2000 ceiling and 6 miles.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And a little trivia gem tucked in the note — the FAF altitude for most Vancouver approaches is 3000 feet. Plus, no risk of thunderstorms and no freezing precipitation, forecast or reported.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Vancouver. Lovely city. Terrifyingly specific paperwork. Alright, everybody stretch — because now we do fuel, and fuel is where the exam lives.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Finally. eff oh em 8.3.2.1 — Domestic fuel, 14 see eff are 121.639. Enough to fly to the destination, then to the most distant alternate, then 45 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And if no alternate is required?

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Then it's destination plus 55 minutes at last cruise altitude consumption rate. Forty-five with an alternate. Fifty-five without.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Feel the need — the need for the right fuel number. Domestic — 45 and 55. Now Flag, eff oh em 8.3.2.2, 14 see eff are 121.645, is a whole different animal.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Flag stacks it up like a plate lunch. Fly to the destination, then burn 10% of the total time from departure to destination, then out to the most distant alternate if you need one, then 30 minutes at holding speed at 1500 feet above the destination or alternate.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] So the Flag signature is the ten-percent-of-total-time plus the 30 minutes at 1500 feet. That "30 at 1500" is how you tell Flag from Domestic in your sleep.

speaker: Pualani
text: [excited] And then the international flavor — eff oh em 8.3.2.3, Special Fuel Reserves, the B043 program on the seven-eight-seven.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] This is our widebody's world. B043 — destination, then 10% of the planned time in oceanic or remote continental airspace — not total time, just the oceanic and remote part — then most distant alternate if required, then 45 minutes at normal cruising consumption, calculated at the flight's weight and altitude at top of descent.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And here's the tell on the seven-eight-seven release. The fuel summary lists "10% RSV" either way — but the differentiator prints right next to it. Standard flag prints "30 at 1500." B043 prints "45 at CRZ." So you read the reserve line and the paper tells you which rule you're flying. Sweet as.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Okay, Chester, this is the one I wanted. Tell 'em about a time redispatch actually saved the day. The fuel-save. And take us out of the hub — Honolulu to Haneda.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] Ohh, the HNL-HND save. Alright. Overwater, Honolulu to Tokyo-Haneda, seven-eight-seven, flag rules, effectively the whole leg is oceanic — so that 10% reserve is riding on a big chunk of Pacific, and 10% of a long crossing is a lot of gas you'd rather sell as payload. So Dispatch builds it as a planned redispatch. eff oh em 8.5.9. Two plans, one flight — the eff ay ay-authorized way to trim that 10% requirement.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Two plans, one flight. Original release to an intermediate destination, and a second plan from a redispatch waypoint out to the intended destination — Haneda. And the waypoint's got to be specified on the original release and common to both routes.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] Right. So we launch heavy but not stupid-heavy, because the reserve only has to cover the intermediate plan, not the whole way. We coast out past the islands, everything's nominal, and within two hours of the redispatch point Dispatch runs the fresh Flight Plan and the numbers are gorgeous. Pacific tailwind came in better than forecast.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] And the timing rule everybody quotes — within two hours, but no later than 20 minutes prior to the waypoint, the destination alternate could be removed from the redispatch plan, because Haneda met the no-alternate requirements at our window.

speaker: Chester
text: [excited] We concurred by ay cars before the point, redispatched to Haneda, and landed with exactly the reserves we're supposed to and not a drop of dead weight hauled across the ocean. That, Otto, is elegant. And here's a bit of trivia for the checkride — the eff oh em literally prints a redispatch sample at 8.5.9.2, and the route they chose for the textbook example is Seattle to Lihue. Seattle to Lihue, in the book, forever.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] It is elegant. And I note — for planned redispatch to and from Hawaii, the flight still has to depart with an alternate for the intended destination. You don't leave the gate bare and hope. You leave covered and get to trim it enroute.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Exactly. And one more from 8.5.9.1 — if routing gets modified so you'll bypass the redispatch point, redispatch is still authorized without further planning as long as the route stays within 100 nautical miles of the planned route. Two hours, twenty minutes, a hundred miles. Those are your redispatch numbers.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] Two, twenty, a hundred. I'll allow it. That's a third clean mnemonic, Pualani. Tally check — Pualani, three. Otto, nil. This is becoming a rout.

speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Chee-hoo. Okay, quick real-world one — eff oh em 8.3.1.2, departure fuel. If you want more gas, the Flight Crew should contact Dispatch at least 30 minutes prior to pushback.

speaker: Chester
text: [serious] And both parties must agree before the extra fueling begins. But if you can't reach concurrence — the Captain has the final decision for fuel on board the aircraft.

text: [dry] As it should be. The Captain's name is the one on the report if it goes pear-shaped. Speaking of pear-shaped — Pualani, tell 'em about your amendment-mid-taxi story. That one still makes me wince.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] [laughs] Okay okay. Honolulu. We're on a seven-eight-seven, pushed back off the gate, engines turning, taxiing out for a westbound departure, and the ay cars chimes. Dispatch. A fast-moving front just put our first alternate in the tank, and they're swapping our alternate and bumping our required fuel. Right there on the taxiway at HNL.

text: [serious] And per eff oh em 8.5.1.4, an alternate change and a required-fuel change are both on the amendment list. So that's not a shrug-and-go. That's a new or amended release.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And 8.5.1.3 — if it becomes necessary to change the conditions of the release, the Dispatcher forwards an amended release, and the Captain acknowledges. Verbally over Company comms, or by acknowledging the ay cars message with the amended info, or a signed copy where paper's required.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] So we stopped. We did not keep rolling. Captain read it, we confirmed the new fuel figure would still be covered, acknowledged the amendment by ay cars — and because the required fuel went up, we actually pulled out of the taxi flow and went back for gas. speaker: Otto
text: [dry] The unglamorous save. No hero music. No flyby. Just a crew that stopped rolling and read the fine print. That's the job.

text: [warm] Now some planning odds and ends that love to show up on tests. eff oh em 8.3.6 — autopilot inoperative. Otto, this one's yours by birthright.

text: [laughs] Otto, explaining the autopilot rule, is a delight I did not know I needed.

text: [dry] Somebody has to add altitude to this conversation. Three-point-five hours, all autopilots dead, you need Captain and Dispatcher sign-off. Under that? speaker: Pualani
text: [laughs] Okay, eff oh em 8.3.5, minimum flight attendants. For the seven-eight-seven, the eff ay ay minimum for boarding and deplaning is 8, and for thru-flights it's "all assigned." Big cabin, big number. Know your ship.

speaker: Otto
text: [dry] And eff oh em 8.3.10.2 — ay are eff eff, rescue and firefighting. For passenger ops you can go one level lower than the aircraft's index at the destination — an Index C aircraft into an Index B field. But for an alternate, the floor is ay are eff eff Index A, eye kay oh category 4.

text: [serious] And a difference of more than one ay are eff eff level at the destination needs DO approval before you operate in or out of there. That's your guardrail.

speaker: Pualani
text: [warm] Good. Now weather for dispatch — eff oh em 8.4.1.4. This table gets misread constantly.

text: [serious] Flight time under one hour — mee tar and taff, both, for dispatch. Flight time one hour or more — the taff controls, mee tar not controlling, for dispatch prior to departure.

text: [dry] But enroute, if you're possibly changing destination, it's always mee tar and taff regardless of flight time. The mee tar comes back into your life the moment you're airborne and reconsidering your choices. Which, over the South Pacific, is roughly hourly.

text: [excited] And winds — eff oh em 8.4.4. Maximum steady-state wind velocity for takeoff and landing is 50 knots. And for dispatch, you use steady-state wind velocity for the crosswind computation.

text: [dry] Fifty knots steady-state and you're already having a genuinely bad day. That's a "hit the brakes and he'll fly right by" kind of wind.

text: [laughs] Two Top Gun in one episode, we scoring. Eh Chester — quick one, you get a 1-2-3 story of your own tucked in Portland?

text: [dry] The 1-2-3 rule holding the line in a Pacific Northwest marine layer. I refuse to be charmed. I am, a little, but I refuse.

text: [dry] And altimeters, eff oh em 8.4.2.5 — settings are rarely outside 28.00 to 32.00 inches of mercury. You can operate below 28 or above 32 only if the altimeter can be set and performance data is available. Otherwise, no. The mercury has opinions.

text: [warm] And missing weather, eff oh em 8.4.2.3 — dispatching to an international or military field that's missing ceiling, visibility, or present weather in the mee tar. text: [dry] And on documents — eff oh em 8.5.1.1 — the certificate holder retains the Dispatch Release, the Flight Plan, and the weather package for three months. Three months. Somewhere, a server remembers your Tuesday.

text: [dry] Surely the Dispatcher decides. [dry] And no — the Captain decides. And don't call me Shirley.
